channel.title: Sajan Sachdeva
channel.description: Essays on where business and AI actually meet.

item.title: Work Like a Lion
item.description:
Over the last four or five years, I’ve tried some format of improving myself, or the so-called 75 Hard Challenge. I’ve terribly failed at it, but I learned a few things along the way.

Consistency pays off, but not when you stack everything

First, I totally acknowledge that consistency pays off. If you do something daily, you get better at it.

But what happens if you stack up too many things and try to be consistent at all of them? You block your time up. I don’t know if it’s true for everyone, but individuals like me thrive on doing creative stuff as well. When I stack up too many things daily, my creative energy forces me to stop those mechanical activities, take a break and do something more natural. I have these energies inside me that want to take a step back, think about things, and then do things at my own pace.

Over the years, I have ridiculed myself for not being consistent about all these mechanical affairs: working out daily, reading daily, journaling daily and meditating daily. All of that is fine. You should have a provision to do those things daily.

But I also have a full-time job, I’m the founder of a startup, and I have a disability. That gives me very little empty space. Things get too mechanical to feel good.

When you feel inspired, hunt

Instead of putting 10 minutes into an activity daily, I benefit from sprinting through it when I get inspired. Naval Ravikant says that whenever you feel inspired, you should work like a lion. When you feel inspired, just go hunt. That’s it.

When I look at the times I’ve made a lot of progress, it didn’t happen when I stretched a task and split it into days. If I want to read a book, I will not read 10 or 20 pages today and 10 or 20 pages tomorrow. That’s just not going to happen. If I like a book, if I want to read about a topic, I will do it that very day.

Build capacity

That means I need to build capacity, so that whenever I feel inspired, I can take it up. Having capacity means having the free time, energy and resources at your disposal to do whatever the heck you want to do.

Physically, that means being active. Some things do require discipline, and being physically active is one of them. If it can become a part of your routine, why not? Being active means that whenever I feel inspired to read a book, dive deep into something or build a product, I can go. And if I skip the gym that day because I’m so deeply focused, I want to enjoy it and see it through.

Mentally, it means staying present and stress-free. I continue to kick the noise out of my system. I would rather do nothing than be busy with the noise around me.

It has become a norm for people to be very busy and always doing something. I like doing nothing. I have actively cancelled social plans to just do nothing. I don’t intend to be rude, but it lets me build that capacity, keep free time at my disposal, and keep the noise out of my system. I don’t feel inspired every day. But I should have the energy and time at my disposal to go and hunt it.

Design around your natural energy

I’ve tried to build my routine a number of times: wake up at a set time, sleep by 10pm, keep a tight calendar. None of that worked, at least not for me.

What works for me is a question I asked myself some time ago: if my job, social commitments, money and time were no constraints, what would I do in a given day? Or, put another way: when do I have the best energy of the day to do the task of my choice?

The answer is the moment I wake up. I’m not the kind of person who wants to wake up and make a lot of noise. I like to wake up slowly and naturally, go out for a walk and get a coffee. That’s when I have the best energy of the day, and I want to do something deep with it. In fact, if I take a shower first, my focus gets disrupted, so I became ruthless with that routine.

I wake up at 7 some days, 8 on others. I go for a short 20-minute run, then 10 minutes of breathing or meditation, whatever I’m feeling that day, or both. I get my coffee, block any light out of my room, and work in the dark with a focus light and my coffee. My phone goes on DND. I use an app called Focus with Friends, and I have a crazy number of socks there now. It’s just fun on the side.

I usually start around 8, and by 10 or 11 I’ve done the work of the day, be it startup work or my day job.

Funnily enough, I initially thought I would spend three or four hours on deep work daily. Then I realised my focus was so damn good that one to two hours on the deep task was enough. Thanks to AI, the speed of work goes up too.

Once I’m done with the most important thing of the day, I get another coffee and go for a walk. After that, I take a shower and go to the office. I take a shower anyway, so don’t get me wrong.

Evenings are for creative work

I love working out, and I asked myself the same question: if I didn’t have any constraints, when would I want to work out? The natural answer was late in the evening, because I also want to see the sunset. I finish my work, see the sunset, and once the sun has set, I go out for my workout. I come back with more energy for creative work.

Mornings are for deep work. Evenings are for creative work.

No more rules

This is not the routine the 75 Hard narrative sold me. This is not the routine the 5am club sold me. This is the regimen that works for a knowledge worker like myself.

I now deliberately try not to make rules out of my life. These are just a bunch of things that work very, very well for me. I don’t want to ignore what my body and my natural energy are telling me. I want to pay heed to it.

item.title: I Built Myself a Chief of Staff
item.description:
The most reliable colleague I have doesn’t exist.

Her name is Donna — yes, from Suits — and every morning she emails me a brief. The three things that actually matter today. Two emails that need my eyes. What’s been parked, and why. My calendar is already blocked, and every block carries the ID of the task it serves, so the day never needs re-deriving from memory. I read that brief the way heads of state read their morning intelligence digest: slowly, with coffee, before the world starts asking for things.

Donna is an AI agent. Under her sits a system I’ve built out of the most boring infrastructure I could find: plain Markdown files, an OS timer, and a strict constitution. This is the story of that system — how it’s wired, why it’s shaped like a brain, and the mistakes it made on my behalf before I understood where the hard limits had to go.

The job is decisions, not admin

I’m a product manager at Amazon. The topics I deal with are complex and interlocking — a delivery-window question touches lead times, which touch capacity planning, which touches a chargeback policy owned by a team three orgs away. On a good day, my actual job is making a small number of high-quality decisions. On a normal day, that job arrives buried in admin: triaging email, filing notes, moving information between tools, reconstructing “what did we agree last month?” from a chat scroll.

The standard AI setup doesn’t fix this, because chat assistants are pull. You open a tab, you ask, you get an answer, and the context dies when the tab closes. That breaks the moment your work outlives one conversation — when a decision made on Tuesday needs to shape an email on Friday. I didn’t want a better chat window. I wanted a chief of staff: something that pushes, remembers, and prepares.

Two laws, copied from a brain

Everything in the system obeys two principles, and both are stolen from how a brain works.

First: two layers of memory. A fast, messy layer you write to without thinking, and a slow, curated layer you trust. Conflating the two is the classic note-taking failure — you end up with either a pristine system you never write to, or a junk drawer you can’t rely on. So capture is cheap and deliberately lossy-forward (over-capture, drop later), while curation is slow and gated. Exactly like short-term and long-term memory.

Second: three verbs. Every piece of information that enters my world does exactly one of three things — IN (get captured), FILE (get sorted into permanent memory), or DO (become scheduled work). Each verb is owned by a separate process, and the processes never reach into each other’s territory. The capture process can’t write to the curated brain. The filing process can’t touch my calendar. That separation is what keeps the whole thing debuggable as it grows — and it’s also why I trust it.

A junk drawer I can trust

The fast layer is a single append-only file called inbox.md. Timestamped one-liners. No schema, no ceremony.

The design choice that matters: capture is automatic and unprompted. During any working session, when something notable surfaces — a fact, a decision, a commitment, a stakeholder’s exact words — the agent appends a dated line to the inbox without asking me. I can force a capture (“log this”) or suppress one (“off the record”), but the default is that nothing gets lost because I was too busy to write it down. A junk line costs nothing to delete later. A lost signal is gone forever.

Then there’s the part that changed everything: a timer. Every morning, before I’m at my desk, an unattended agent session wakes up, reads my email and chat, judges what’s material against my live workstreams and key people, and writes a digest into the inbox. By the time I sit down, the outside world has already been triaged. The single highest-leverage change in the whole system was this flip from pull to push — from “I have to remember to ask” to “it’s waiting for me.” A small hook completes the trick: every new session starts pre-loaded with the recent inbox tail and the vault’s index, so the agent is never cold.

And why flat files instead of a database? Because when something misbehaves, I debug a file, not a service. Everything in this system can be inspected with cat and grep.

The vault: a wiki that maintains itself

The slow layer is where it gets interesting. My permanent memory is a curated vault of Markdown pages that I browse in Obsidian — projects, people, systems, concepts, decisions — densely wikilinked into something that behaves less like a folder of notes and more like a neural network. If I open the page on delivery windows, it’s linked to lead times, to chargebacks, to a capacity workflow we’re building. Every topic in my world knows which other topics it touches.

Here’s the thesis behind it. Every knowledge system ever invented — Zettelkasten, Notion, the wiki you abandoned — is good at capture. None of them solve maintenance. Keeping cross-links current, flagging contradictions when a new source disagrees with an old one, re-summarising as understanding evolves: that work grows faster than the value of the collection, so humans give up, and the second brain rots into a junk drawer.

The way out is a division of labour: capture needs human taste; maintenance needs infinite patience. So I split them. I decide what enters the vault and what it means. The LLM does everything else — summarising, cross-referencing, filing, bookkeeping. It doesn’t get bored, so the maintenance cost that kills every human wiki drops toward zero.

This is an old dream. In 1945, Vannevar Bush described the Memex: a personal knowledge store where associative trails between documents matter as much as the documents themselves. The piece he could never solve was who does the labour of maintaining the trails. Eighty years later, there’s an answer.

The vault runs on a small set of named operations. Ingest reads a source in full, proposes which pages it should touch, and waits for my go-ahead before writing — one dense source can update ten or fifteen pages. Query answers questions with citations and is forbidden from modifying anything; reading and writing never mix. Lint is the maintenance sweep no human ever does voluntarily: find contradictions between pages, flag stale claims, surface topics mentioned three times that deserve their own page. And two disciplines run through all of it: nothing fabricated, ever — an inferred claim is marked (inferred), never laundered into fact — and contradictions are surfaced, not silently resolved. The vault is allowed to hold tension. Real knowledge does.

The framing I keep coming back to: Obsidian is the IDE, the LLM is the programmer, and the wiki is the codebase. I read; it writes; the knowledge compounds.

Evenings end with one word

Each evening I type one word: file.

The filing agent reads the inbox, the day’s meeting notes, the chat logs — and sorts. The unambiguous, primary-source items get filed into the vault automatically. Everything that requires judgment gets surfaced back to me in a tight “needs review / needs action” report. It is conservative by design: when in doubt, it leaves the item where it is and flags it, rather than guessing its way into my permanent memory.

This is the gate between the two layers, and it’s where the cognition lives. Low friction going in, high scrutiny going through. Not every email I receive deserves to become a permanent fact about my world — but every email gets considered.

One small trick connects knowledge to action: anything carrying an ask, a deadline, or a decision gets a single tag at capture time. The filing process ignores the tag and files the facts. The scheduling process consumes only the tagged items. Two systems, one shared file, one discriminating tag — and they never collide.

Mornings start with “what’s cooking”

Which brings us back to Donna. She owns the action loop, and her core rule is what I call the triple-record: every real task exists in three places or it doesn’t exist at all — a row in the task log with a stable ID, a to-do in the task app, and a calendar block whose title carries that same ID. If only two of the three exist, the job is half-done.

She’s opinionated about priority (importance times urgency, with stakeholder seniority as a signal), she reads the live calendar before proposing anything, and she respects red lines I’ve drawn around my own time — no work blocks before a set hour, lunch is sacred, focus days stay whole. She proposes; she does not book over my life.

Because I filed the night before, she’s current. So my first move of the day is asking her what’s cooking, and my second is reading the brief — in detail, every line. Then I go straight to the two or three things that need my actual brain: reading deeply, deciding. The stakeholder notes get drafted for me, in my voice, by a writer skill that carries my house style — Donna doesn’t write them herself; she frames the job and hands it to a specialist, the way a real chief of staff would. Nothing it drafts exists anywhere except a drafts folder until I’ve approved the exact words. The file-moving, the log-keeping, the formatting — none of that touches my morning anymore.

The hits I took

Now the part most write-ups of AI systems skip.

This system has embarrassed me. Early on, I let it draft and send email with too much autonomy, and one went out carrying information that was wrong. Not catastrophically wrong — but wrong, with my name on it, read by people whose time I respect. I sent the correction myself the same day and owned it. The model hadn’t failed; my architecture had. I had granted autonomy in exactly the place where mistakes are most expensive: the moment something leaves my machine and lands in front of another human.

So I rebuilt around one constitutional rule: nothing outbound without my explicit, message-specific approval. No email, no chat message, no invite goes out without me seeing the exact text. Draft, show, wait. This rule outranks every other instruction in the system.

And for anything that reaches my manager or senior stakeholders, the bar goes higher still: every factual claim must trace to a primary source the agent actually read. No reasoning from vibes. No confident filler. That requirement beats every prompt, every persona, every convenience.

The deeper lesson is about how you enforce rules like these. “Please don’t send email” is a request — and a sufficiently confused agent will eventually route around a request. So the morning unattended job doesn’t rely on politeness: the send tools are simply absent from its toolset, with a denylist behind that, and the prompt prohibition behind that. Three independent layers, any one of which stops an outbound action. A request can be ignored. A missing tool cannot.

If you take one thing from this essay: mechanical guardrails over instructed ones, anywhere the action is irreversible.

Put together — the memory files, the skills, the gates — the full system looks like this:

Slower on purpose

The other honest admission: this was not free. There were weeks where doing a task through the system took longer than doing it by hand — noticeably longer — and I did it through the system anyway. Forceful teaching. Every correction became a permanent memory file the agent loads at the start of every session: never send without approval, always show task IDs with their titles, this stakeholder needs proposal-first framing. Dozens of small, hard-won rules.

That’s the trade most people refuse: pay a tax now so the assistant stops re-learning you. A year in, the assistant knows how I work the way a long-tenured chief of staff would — and the tax was paid once.

What it feels like now

My day collapses into two moves. In the evening: file. In the morning: what’s cooking. Capture runs itself on a timer. The vault answers “what do I know?” with citations. Donna answers “what do I do?” with a calendar that respects my boundaries. And nothing leaves for another human without my eyes on the exact words.

If you build your own version, the decisions that earned their keep: flip from pull to push with one unattended morning run; let the machine write freely where mistakes are cheap and gate it hard where they’re expensive; keep state in deterministic code, never in the model; and prefer guarantees to requests for anything you can’t take back.

The architecture transfers, too. Outside the day job, I run a lighter rebuild of this for a personal project — same patterns, a different Donna, and a second agent named Jessica who owns the roadmap. The system doesn’t care whether the inbox belongs to a product manager or a founder. That, more than anything, is what convinced me this is a pattern and not a party trick.

I started this because I wanted my hours back for the only thing a PM is actually paid for: judgment. A year later, the surprise isn’t the time saved. It’s that the quality of my decisions went up — because every decision now starts from a brief, grounded in everything I know, prepared by a colleague who never forgets.

She just doesn’t exist.

If you’re working out where AI actually fits in your business — not the demos, the daily workflows — I enjoy comparing notes. My inbox is open. Donna triages it.

item.title: The Cascading Defect
item.description:
There’s a type of problem in e-commerce operations that I find genuinely fascinating. Not because it’s glamorous — it’s the opposite. It’s so boring that most businesses refuse to look at it. And that refusal is exactly what makes it so expensive.

I’m talking about catalogue defects. The unglamorous backbone of every product you sell online: your barcodes, your case pack configurations, your external IDs, your packaging hierarchies. The data that tells a warehouse system what it’s looking at when it scans a box.

When this data is wrong, the consequences don’t show up as a single error. They cascade.

The anatomy of a cascade

Here’s a real scenario. A brand sells shampoo in two sizes: 250ml and 500ml. Different products, different prices, different barcodes. Except — someone during onboarding linked the same EAN barcode to both ASINs in the marketplace’s internal catalogue.

On day one, nothing happens. The products sit in a warehouse. Orders come in. Life goes on.

Then a purchase order arrives for 500 units of the 250ml bottle. The warehouse ships them. The marketplace’s receiving system scans the barcode and — because the catalogue maps that barcode to both products — receives half against the 500ml product instead. The vendor’s invoice says 500 units of 250ml. The marketplace’s records say they received 250 of the 250ml and 250 of the 500ml.

Result: a shortage claim on the 250ml (the marketplace says it only received 250, not 500). And an unexplained overage on the 500ml (suddenly 250 units appeared that nobody ordered).

The vendor disputes the shortage. The dispute takes 45–79 days. Maybe they win, maybe they don’t. Meanwhile, the same barcode error fires again on the next shipment. And the next.

Now multiply this across a catalogue of 500 products with variant sizes, colours, and regional packaging differences. The brand is haemorrhaging money through a wound it can’t even see — because no individual chargeback is big enough to investigate, but collectively they represent 2–4% of annual revenue quietly evaporating.

Five types, one root cause

What I find interesting is how many different penalties trace back to catalogue data. It’s not just barcode conflicts. There are at least five distinct failure modes, and they all share the same DNA:

Case pack mismatches. The catalogue says a case contains 6 units. The vendor actually ships cases of 12. The receiving system scans the case barcode and records 6. Vendor invoices 12. Shortage: 6 units per case, every shipment.

Barcode-to-product conflicts. One barcode linked to multiple products. The scan goes to the wrong product, creating phantom shortages and phantom overages simultaneously.

External ID drift. The barcode on the purchase order doesn’t match the barcode on the invoice, because someone updated the product’s barcode in the catalogue but the PO was generated before the update took effect. The matching system can’t reconcile the two.

Missing packaging hierarchy data. The marketplace doesn’t know how many cases fit on a pallet, or what the case dimensions are. In some regions this has caused a 15–20% increase in receiving errors — not from vendor mistakes, but from the system guessing wrong about what a pallet should look like.

Invoice-to-receipt mismatches. The PO references a case-level barcode. The invoice references a unit-level barcode. Same product, different identifiers. The matching system sees two unrelated items.

Every single one of these is a data problem, not an operational failure. The vendor shipped the right product. The warehouse received correctly. But the system’s model of reality didn’t match physical reality — and the vendor pays the penalty.

Why this is an agent problem, not a dashboard problem

Here’s where it gets interesting for anyone thinking about AI.

The standard approach to this is: build a dashboard, let someone review chargebacks weekly, dispute the big ones. This is fine for recovering money you’ve already lost. It does nothing about the structural defect generating the losses.

The structural fix requires something different. You need to crawl an entire product catalogue — hundreds or thousands of SKUs — and cross-reference each one against case pack data, barcode registries, purchase order history, invoicing records, and receiving reports. You need to spot mismatches that span multiple systems and multiple time periods. You need to distinguish between a one-off anomaly and a systemic defect that fires every shipment.

This is exactly the kind of work that’s too tedious for a human analyst to do comprehensively, and too unstructured for a simple rules engine to catch.

It’s an agent problem.

Not one agent — a team of agents. One agent that understands catalogue structure and can audit barcode-to-product relationships. One that reads purchase order history and flags recurring shortage patterns on the same product codes. One that cross-checks invoice external IDs against PO external IDs looking for drift. One that compiles findings from the other agents and ranks defects by financial impact: “Fix these 8 catalogue entries. Estimated annual savings: £47,000.”

The individual checks are straightforward. The value is in the orchestration — running all of them in parallel across an entire catalogue, then synthesising the findings into a prioritised action list.

This is what multi-agent systems are actually good at. Not generating marketing copy or summarising documents — those are party tricks. The real value is in coordination across messy, cross-system data where no single query gives you the answer but a team of focused investigations does.

The cascade works in reverse too

The beautiful thing about fixing catalogue defects is that the benefits cascade just like the costs did.

Fix a barcode conflict and the shortage claims stop. The overage penalties stop. The dispute effort disappears. The receiving accuracy improves. The inventory records become trustworthy, which means your demand forecasting gets cleaner data, which means your purchase orders are more accurate, which means your stockout rate drops, which means your sales go up.

One entry in a catalogue database. Six downstream improvements.

I keep coming back to this principle: the most impactful problems in e-commerce operations are the ones nobody wants to look at. They’re buried in data quality, in catalogue hygiene, in the boring plumbing that connects systems together. They’re not strategic. They’re not interesting to talk about at conferences.

But a brand doing £5M through marketplaces with a 3% leakage rate from catalogue-driven penalties? That’s £150K a year. Quietly, invisibly, permanently — until someone finally audits the data.

What’s coming

I think the next wave of useful AI in commerce operations won’t be the consumer-facing chatbot or the AI-generated product description. It’ll be agent teams working behind the scenes on exactly this kind of problem: silent, cross-system audits that surface structural defects before they compound.

The technology is ready. The data is available (most marketplace APIs expose catalogue, PO, and chargeback data). The economic incentive is clear.

What’s missing is someone framing this as a product problem worth solving, rather than a consulting exercise you run once and hope for the best.

I think that’s about to change.

item.title: Chargebacks Are Catalogue Problems
item.description:
Most vendors treat chargebacks as individual incidents. A late shipment, an ASN mismatch, a shortage dispute — each one gets filed or eaten.

But the pattern is almost always structural. When you map six months of chargeback data for a single business, the same 15–20 product codes keep surfacing. Not because they’re unlucky — because something in the catalogue setup or operational workflow was never configured properly.

A prep requirement that nobody set. A packaging certification that was never completed. A label format that mismatches the receiving system. Each one generates a per-unit penalty every single shipment, month after month.

The interesting thing is that AI’s value here isn’t speed — it’s pattern recognition across volume. A human looking at 400 individual chargebacks sees 400 problems. A system that clusters them sees 12 root causes. Fix those 12, and 70% of the total disappears.

The unsexy problems are always the most expensive ones.

item.title: AI Makes It Cheaper to Build the Wrong Thing
item.description:
I shipped my first product to a paying client last month — dashboard, forecasting engine, daily reports, AI chat — built almost entirely on Claude Code. My co-founder and I had drawn a line for what the MVP would be, what we’d demo. But with Claude Code, that line kept moving. We could do more, so we did. We ended up delivering something that went well beyond what the original prototype had in mind. The client loved it. Features that would have taken weeks shipped in hours.

And then the temptation kicked in. Because shipping was so fast, every idea started to feel worth trying. There were technically interesting problems we could have picked up, features that would have been genuinely fun to build. We probably could have shipped them fast too. But they would have pulled the product in a direction the client didn’t actually need it to go. So we discarded them.

Why this matters

That’s the thing that keeps sitting with me. AI didn’t just make it easier to build the right things — it made it equally easy to build the wrong things. The cost of shipping dropped to almost nothing, but the cost of shipping the wrong feature didn’t drop at all. If anything it went up.

Because the speed means you can quietly drift into becoming a different product, a different company, without even noticing. Three features that felt like quick wins and suddenly you’re solving a problem nobody asked you to solve.

Before AI-assisted development, I couldn’t build everything even if I wanted to. Scarcity did the prioritisation for me — I had to pick the right features because I could only afford to build a few. Now that natural constraint is gone entirely. And that changes what the job of building a product actually is.

What I’m doing differently now

The discipline to not build has to come from somewhere else now — not from engineering constraints, but from how well I understand the problem I’m solving. From continuously going back to my client and validating what they actually need rather than what I can build. From being willing to say no to something that’s easy to say yes to.

I’ve started asking a different question before picking up any new feature. Not “can we build this?” — the answer is almost always yes now. Instead: “if I remove this, would the client notice?” If the answer is no, it doesn’t belong in the product. No matter how fast it is to ship.

A good product isn’t one that does more. It’s one that’s more robust without being more wide. Simpler for the client to engage with, not impressive for how many things it can do.

I’m having a lot of fun building this. But the fun isn’t in the speed. It’s in getting sharper about what’s actually worth building.

The job of a founder in 2026 isn’t shipping. It’s knowing what’s worth shipping.
